newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sees few gains from greater labour flexibility.
newsitem.headline: EU sees few gains from greater labour flexibility.

text.p: European Union efforts to stimulate jobs growth through more flexible labour markets have not realised their full potential, the European Commission said on Wednesday in its annual review of employment trends.
With nearly 11 percent of the EU's workforce unemployed, EU governments have been under considerable public pressure to do more to boost employment.
Yet the Commission's report, noting that there was a rising trend towards reducing labour market rigidities, said the benefits were largely seen in an expansion of part-time work.
In particular, the report said the difficulties of creating more secure full-time employment were related to "the way enterprises go about the reorganisation of production and working arrangements.
"Such measures are often confined to changes at the margin of the workforce through expanding use of outsourcing, temporary work contracts and atypical work arrangements," the report added.
The Commission emphasised that a continued trend towards flexibility should not come at the expense of social security, a clear desire to avoid a replication of the U.S. labour market model.
The report also called for greater investment in the physical productive capacity of economies, intellectual know-how, infrastructure and knowledge and skills.
The Commission also made the following observations.
-- Long term unemployment is the intractable element of the jobless problem in the EU, with over 50 percent of those out work in 1995 considered chronically unemployed.

-- Over the 1988-1995 period, companies with fewer than 100 employees increased net employment at a rate of 259,000 per year, while companies with more than 100 employees had net job losses of 222,250 per year.
-- The services sector provided most of the net addition of jobs in 1995, while the decline in employment in agriculture and industry continued.
-- The number of people working at night and at weekends has increased almost everywhere. Most of the new jobs created in 1995 were part-time.
-- Youth unemployment is still twice as high as that of adults, at over 20 percent on average.

-- Women have accounted for the entire growth of the labour force in the last 20 years. The rate of joblesness among women, which stood at 12.5 percent in July 1996, has been unaffected by the economic recovery and remains higher than that for men in all but two of the EU's 15 nations.
